q: What is the value of 1/4 + 1/2?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 4: 1/4 stays as it is and 1/2 = 2/4. Add the tops: 1 + 2 = 3, giving 3/4.
traps: Added the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get added.
Multiplied the two fractions (tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms) when the sign says to add.
Too big by 1/2. This is what 1/4 + 2/2 would give, so one numerator slipped by one during the conversion.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 2/3 + 3/4?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 12: 2/3 = 8/12 and 3/4 = 9/12. Add the tops: 8 + 9 = 17, giving 17/12.
traps: Added the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get added.
Put both over 12 but kept the old tops. When the bottom is scaled up, the top has to be scaled by the same factor.
This is the correct value turned upside down. Keep the common denominator on the bottom.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 5/6 − 1/4?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 12: 5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12. Subtract the tops: 10 - 3 = 7, giving 7/12.
traps: Subtracted the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get subtracted.
Used 24 as the denominator but kept the old tops. Each top must be scaled along with its bottom.
Added the fractions when the sign says to subtract.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: 3 1/4 + 2 2/3 = ? (mixed numbers)
why: Add the whole numbers and the fractions separately. Wholes: 3 + 2 = 5. Fractions over 12: 1/4 = 3/12 and 2/3 = 8/12, which add to 11/12. Total: 5 11/12.
traps: Added the fraction tops and bottoms straight across (1 + 2 over 4 + 3).
The fraction part is right, but the wholes 3 + 2 make 5. Nothing carries because 11/12 is under 1.
Used 12 as the denominator but kept the old tops, 1 + 2. Scale each top with its bottom: 3/12 and 8/12.
trick: Mixed numbers: handle wholes and fractions separately, then carry only if the fraction part reaches 1.

q: What is 3/8 written as a decimal?
why: 1/8 = 0.125, so 3/8 is three of those: 0.375.
traps: Rounded. 3/8 ends exactly at 0.375, and that exact value is offered.
Cut off after one digit. 0.3 is 3/10, a different fraction.
trick: Memorize the unit fractions (1/4 = 0.25, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/6 = 0.167, 1/8 = 0.125) and build the rest by multiplying.

q: What is 5/8 written as a decimal?
why: 1/8 = 0.125, and five of those make 0.625. Size check: 5/8 is a bit more than 1/2.
traps: Writes the digits 5 and 8 after a decimal point. A fraction is a division: 5 divided by 8.
That is 3/8.
A near guess. Eighths land on 0.625: five times 0.125.
That is 3/5. It rounds too far, and the exact value is offered.
trick: Memorize the unit fractions (1/4 = 0.25, 1/5 = 0.2, 1/6 = 0.167, 1/8 = 0.125) and build the rest by multiplying.

q: Which is bigger: 3/7 or 0.43?
What is 15% of 80?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 15% of 80 is 0.15 x 80 = 12. Mental route: 10% of 80 is 8, and 1% is 0.8; build 15% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 80.
20 is 25% of 80, not 15%. Anchor on 10% of 80 = 8.
8 is 10% of 80, not 15%. Anchor on 10% of 80 = 8.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 40% of 250?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 40% of 250 is 0.4 x 250 = 100. Mental route: 10% of 250 is 25, and 1% is 2.5; build 40% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 250.
62.5 is 25% of 250, not 40%. Anchor on 10% of 250 = 25.
125 is 50% of 250, not 40%. Anchor on 10% of 250 = 25.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 8% of 50?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 8% of 50 is 0.08 x 50 = 4. Mental route: 10% of 50 is 5, and 1% is 0.5; build 8% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 50.
Decimal point one place too far left. Check: 10% of 50 is already 5.
Decimal point one place too far right. Check: 10% of 50 is only 5.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: A $50 shirt is marked up 20%. New price?
why: 20% of $50 is $10. A markup adds it: $50 + $10 = $60. One step: 50 x 1.20.
traps: Treated 20% as 20 dollars. Take 20% of $50 first, which is $10.
This is only the markup. Add it to the original price.
The price went down. A markup raises it.
trick: Turn the change into one multiplier: up 30% is x 1.30, down 30% is x 0.70.

q: A $200 jacket is on sale for 35% off. Sale price?
traps: Treated 35% as 35 dollars. 35% of $200 is $70.
This is the discount, not the sale price.
That is 30% off. 35% of $200 is $70, not $60.
trick: Turn the change into one multiplier: up 30% is x 1.30, down 30% is x 0.70.

q: A jar held 80 marbles. Now it holds 100. Percent increase?
why: Percent change = change divided by the original. The change is 20 and the original is 80: 20/80 = 0.25 = 25%.
traps: Divided by the new amount (20/100), or reported the raw change of 20 as a percent. The base is the starting value, 80.
This is the new amount as a percent of the old (100/80). The increase is the extra 25%.
15% of 80 is only 12. The jar gained 20.
trick: Percent change always divides by the starting value: (new - old) / old.

q: A $100 item is increased 20%, then decreased 20%. Final price?
why: Up 20%: $100 x 1.2 = $120. Down 20% of the new price: $120 x 0.8 = $96. The cut is taken from a bigger number than the raise was, so you end below the start.
traps: Assumed +20% and -20% cancel. The cut is 20% of $120, which is $24, not $20.
Stopped after the increase.
Applied only the decrease to the original $100.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: A stock rises 10% then rises another 10%. Total percent rise?
why: Multiply the growth factors: 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21, a 21% total rise. The second 10% is earned on the already larger price, which adds the extra point.
traps: Added the two percents. The second 10% applies to 110% of the start, so it is worth 11 points.
This is the price after the first rise as a percent of the start, not the total rise.
Overshoots. The extra from compounding is 10% of 10%, which is 1 point, not 2.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: "Sam has 3 more apples than twice what Mia has." If Mia has m apples, Sam has...
why: Build it from the inside out. 'Twice what Mia has' is 2m. '3 more than' that adds 3: 2m + 3.
traps: 'More than' means add. This takes 3 away.
Merged the 3 and the 2 into 6. 'Twice' multiplies m; '3 more' adds to the result.
Swapped the roles of 3 and 2. 'Twice' gives the multiplier 2, and 3 is the amount added.
trick: Find the base phrase first, then apply 'more than' or 'less than' to it. 'A less than B' reads backward: B - A.

q: "A number is 5 less than half of another." If the second number is n, the first is...
why: 'Half of another' is n/2. '5 less than' that means start with n/2 and take away 5: n/2 - 5.
traps: 'Less than' means subtract, not add.
Order reversed. '5 less than X' is X - 5; the 5 is what gets removed.
Used twice n instead of half of n.
trick: Find the base phrase first, then apply 'more than' or 'less than' to it. 'A less than B' reads backward: B - A.

q: If 3x + 7 = 22, what is the value of x?
why: Undo the operations in reverse order. First subtract 7 from both sides: 3x = 15. Then divide by 3: x = 5.
traps: Substitute it: 3(7) + 7 = 28, not 22.
Stopped at 3x = 15 and never divided by 3.
Substitute it: 3(9) + 7 = 34, not 22.
trick: Solve by undoing: clear the added or subtracted number first, then divide. Substitute your answer to check in five seconds.

q: If 2(x − 3) = x + 4, what is the value of x?
why: Distribute: 2x - 6 = x + 4. Subtract x from both sides: x - 6 = 4. Add 6: x = 10. Check: 2(10 - 3) = 14 and 10 + 4 = 14.
traps: Distributed the 2 only to x (2x - 3 = x + 4). The 2 multiplies the 3 as well.
Sign slip moving the 6: x - 6 = 4 means add 6, which gives 10.
Substitute it: left side 2(1 - 3) = -4, right side 5. They do not match.
trick: Substitute your answer back into the original equation. It takes five seconds and catches sign slips.

q: If (x + 4)/3 = 5, what is the value of x?
why: Undo the division first: multiply both sides by 3 to get x + 4 = 15. Then subtract 4: x = 11.
traps: Stopped at x + 4 = 15. That is the whole numerator; x is 4 less.
Subtracted 4 from 5 before clearing the 3. The whole top is divided by 3, so multiply first.
Added 4 instead of subtracting it after multiplying.
Substitute it: (3 + 4)/3 is 7/3, not 5.
trick: A fraction bar groups the whole numerator. Clear the denominator before touching what is on top.

q: If 4(2x − 1) − 3 = 5x + 2, what is the value of x?
why: Distribute: 8x - 4 - 3 = 5x + 2, so 8x - 7 = 5x + 2. Subtract 5x: 3x - 7 = 2. Add 7: 3x = 9, so x = 3.
traps: Substitute it: left side 4(3) - 3 = 9, right side 12. Not equal.
Substitute it: left side 4(9) - 3 = 33, right side 27. Not equal.
Substitute it: left side 4(-1) - 3 = -7, right side 2. Not equal.
trick: Multi-step equations: distribute, combine like terms on each side, then solve. Substituting each choice is a fast backup.

q: A recipe calls for flour and sugar in ratio 3:2. If you use 12 cups of flour, how much sugar?
why: Flour is 3 parts and equals 12 cups, so one part is 4 cups. Sugar is 2 parts: 2 x 4 = 8 cups.
traps: Halved the flour. In a 3 to 2 ratio, sugar is two thirds of the flour, not half.
Doubled the flour. Sugar is the smaller share in a 3:2 ratio.
This is the size of one part. Sugar is 2 parts.
trick: Ratios: add the parts, find the size of one part, then multiply by the parts you need.

q: In a class, the boy:girl ratio is 5:7. If there are 36 students total, how many boys?
why: 5 + 7 = 12 parts in all. 36 students / 12 parts = 3 students per part. Boys are 5 parts: 15.
traps: That is the girls (7 parts). Match the order of the ratio to the order of the words.
This is the number of parts, not a number of students.
This is the boys' ratio number. Each part is worth 3 students.
trick: Ratios: add the parts, find the size of one part, then multiply by the parts you need.

q: 4 workers paint a wall in 6 hours. How long for 3 workers (same pace)?
why: The job is 4 x 6 = 24 worker-hours. With 3 workers: 24 / 3 = 8 hours. Fewer workers means more time.
traps: Set up a direct proportion (6 x 3/4). Workers and time move in opposite directions.
That would be the time for 2 workers: 24 / 2.
The time cannot stay the same when a worker is removed.
trick: Workers x time = total work. Hold the total fixed and solve.

q: What is the value of log₂(8)?
why: The question is: 2 to what power gives 8? 2 x 2 x 2 = 8, so the power is 3.
traps: This is 8 / 2. A log counts factors of 2, and 2^4 is 16.
Repeats the number inside the log. The log is the exponent.
trick: Rewrite every log as an exponent question: log base b of N = k means b^k = N.

q: What is the value of log₁₀(1000)?
why: 10 to what power gives 1000? 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000, so the answer is 3. With base 10 you can count the zeros.
traps: This is the base. The log is the exponent on it.
This is 1000 / 10. A log counts how many tens multiply together: three.
Repeats the number inside the log.
trick: Rewrite every log as an exponent question: log base b of N = k means b^k = N.

q: What is the value of log₂(1/8)?
why: 2^3 = 8, and a negative exponent means one over: 2^-3 = 1/8. So the log is -3.
traps: 2^3 is 8, not 1/8. A value below 1 needs a negative exponent.
2^(1/3) is the cube root of 2, about 1.26. Reciprocals come from negative exponents, not fractional ones.
Mixed the two ideas. The size of the exponent is 3; only its sign changes.
Put a minus sign on the number itself. The log is an exponent, not the value.
trick: The log of 1/N is the negative of the log of N.

q: If pH = −log[H⁺] and [H⁺] = 10⁻⁵, find pH.
why: log(10^-5) is just the exponent, -5. The formula puts a minus sign in front: pH = -(-5) = 5.
traps: Stopped at log(10^-5) = -5 and forgot the minus sign in the pH formula.
This is the concentration itself. pH is the negative log of it.
Took the log of the exponent's size. The log of 10^-5 is simply -5.
trick: For a concentration of 10^-n, the pH is n.

q: What is the value of log(40) − log(4)?
A bacteria population doubles every hour. If it starts at 100, how many hours to reach 1600?
why: 1600 / 100 = 16, so the population must grow 16-fold. Each hour doubles it: 2, 4, 8, 16. That is 4 doublings, so 4 hours.
traps: This is the growth factor, not the number of hours. 16 = 2^4.
Not a count of doublings. Track it: 200, 400, 800, 1600 is four steps.
Halved 16 instead of asking how many 2s multiply to make 16.
trick: Doubling problems: divide final by start, then count how many 2s multiply to that factor.

q: A car travels at 60 mph for 2.5 hours. How far?
why: Distance = rate x time = 60 x 2.5. Two hours cover 120 miles and the extra half hour covers 30 more: 150 miles.
traps: Counted only 2 hours and dropped the half hour.
This is only the half-hour piece.
Far too short. One hour alone at 60 mph covers 60 miles.
trick: Let the units steer: miles per hour times hours leaves miles; miles divided by hours leaves miles per hour.

q: A train covers 240 miles in 3 hours. What is its speed?
why: Speed = distance / time = 240 / 3 = 80 mph. Check: 80 x 3 = 240.
traps: 60 x 3 = 180, which is short of 240.
Divided by 2 instead of 3.
Multiplied distance by time. Speed is miles per hour, so divide.
70 x 3 = 210, which is short of 240.
trick: Let the units steer: miles per hour times hours leaves miles; miles divided by hours leaves miles per hour.

q: Two cars start 200 miles apart, driving toward each other. One at 50 mph, the other 30 mph. When do they meet?
why: Moving toward each other, the gap closes at the sum of the speeds: 50 + 30 = 80 mph. Time = 200 / 80 = 2.5 hours.
traps: Used only the 50 mph car (200 / 50). Both cars are closing the gap.
In 2 hours they close only 160 of the 200 miles.
Averaged the speeds to 40 mph. Speeds add when objects approach each other.
trick: Toward each other: add the speeds. Same direction: subtract them.

q: What is the value of 1/3 + 1/6?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 6: 1/3 = 2/6 and 1/6 stays as it is. Add the tops: 2 + 1 = 3, giving 3/6, which reduces to 1/2.
traps: Added the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get added.
Used 18 as the denominator but kept the old tops. Each top must be scaled along with its bottom.
Put both over 6 but kept the old tops. When the bottom is scaled up, the top has to be scaled by the same factor.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 7/8 − 1/2?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 8: 7/8 stays as it is and 1/2 = 4/8. Subtract the tops: 7 - 4 = 3, giving 3/8.
traps: Put both over 8 but kept the old tops. When the bottom is scaled up, the top has to be scaled by the same factor.
Put both over 8 but kept the old tops. When the bottom is scaled up, the top has to be scaled by the same factor.
Too big by 1/4 compared with the true value 3/8. Redo the conversion to a denominator of 8 and combine only the tops.

q: What is the value of 2/5 + 1/10?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 10: 2/5 = 4/10 and 1/10 stays as it is. Add the tops: 4 + 1 = 5, giving 5/10, which reduces to 1/2.
traps: Added the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get added.
Added the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get added.
Subtracted the fractions when the sign says to add.

q: What is the value of 3/4 − 1/3 + 1/6?
why: Put everything over 12: 9/12 - 4/12 + 2/12. Work left to right: 9 - 4 = 5, then 5 + 2 = 7. Answer 7/12.
traps: Stopped after the subtraction and never added the 1/6.
Subtracted the last fraction instead of adding it (9 - 4 - 2).
Skipped the subtraction: 9/12 + 2/12.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is 1/4 written as a decimal?
why: One quarter of 1 is 0.25, the way a quarter of a dollar is 25 cents. Division check: 1 divided by 4 = 0.25.
traps: Copies the denominator after the decimal point. 0.4 is 4/10.
Writes the digits 1 and 4 side by side. The fraction bar means divide.
That is 1/2. A quarter is half of a half.
That is 3/4, what is left of the whole after 1/4 is removed.
trick: Tie the benchmarks to money: quarter = 0.25, half = 0.50, three quarters = 0.75.

q: What is 7/8 written as a decimal?
why: 7/8 is one eighth short of a whole: 1 - 0.125 = 0.875.
traps: Writes the digits 7 and 8 after a decimal point. Divide instead: 7 by 8.
That is 1/8, the piece that is missing, not the 7/8 that is present.
Too close to 1. The gap from 1 is a full eighth, 0.125.
That is 6/7. Sevenths and eighths are easy to cross; eighths move in steps of 0.125.
trick: For fractions just under 1, subtract the missing piece from 1.

q: Convert 0.625 to a fraction.
why: 0.625 is 625/1000. Divide top and bottom by 125 to get 5/8. Shortcut: 0.625 is five steps of 0.125, and 0.125 is 1/8.
traps: 5/9 is 0.555..., a repeating decimal. 0.625 stops after three places.
That is 0.6, which drops the extra 0.025.
trick: Three-place decimals ending in 5 are often eighths: 0.125, 0.375, 0.625, 0.875.

q: Which is closer to 0.6: 3/5 or 5/9?
why: 3/5 = 6/10 = 0.6 exactly, so its distance from 0.6 is zero. 5/9 = 0.555..., which is about 0.044 away.
traps: 5/9 is 0.555..., about 0.044 below 0.6. 3/5 hits 0.6 exactly.
Only one of them equals 0.6. Convert both to decimals before comparing.
Both are fixed numbers, so the comparison is settled once you convert them.
trick: To compare fractions with a decimal, convert everything to decimals.

q: What is 10% of 60?
why: 10% means one tenth. One tenth of 60 is 6.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 60.
Decimal point one place too far right. Check: 10% of 60 is only 6.
Decimal point one place too far left. Check: 10% of 60 is already 6.
16 is 26.67% of 60, not 10%. Anchor on 10% of 60 = 6.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 30% of 90?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 30% of 90 is 0.3 x 90 = 27. Mental route: 10% of 90 is 9, and 1% is 0.9; build 30% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 90.
Subtracted the percent from the number as if it were a plain amount.
9 is 10% of 90, not 30%. Anchor on 10% of 90 = 9.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 12% of 50?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 12% of 50 is 0.12 x 50 = 6. Mental route: 10% of 50 is 5, and 1% is 0.5; build 12% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 50.
5 is 10% of 50, not 12%. Anchor on 10% of 50 = 5.
24 is 48% of 50, not 12%. Anchor on 10% of 50 = 5.

q: What is 7.5% of 200?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 7.5% of 200 is 0.075 x 200 = 15. Mental route: 10% of 200 is 20, and 1% is 2; build 7.5% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 200.
Decimal point one place too far right. Check: 10% of 200 is only 20.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: A $40 shirt is 25% off. Sale price?
why: 25% is one quarter, and a quarter of $40 is $10. Sale price: $40 - $10 = $30.
traps: This is the discount (25% of $40). Subtract it from the price.
Treated 25% as 25 dollars off. A quarter of $40 is $10.
The price went up. 'Off' means subtract.
trick: Turn the change into one multiplier: up 30% is x 1.30, down 30% is x 0.70.

q: A salary went from $60K to $66K. % increase?
why: The raise is 6 (thousand) on a starting salary of 60: 6/60 = 0.10 = 10%.
traps: Reported the raw change of 6 as if it were a percent. Divide it by the starting 60.
Divided by the new salary (6/66 is about 9%). The base is the original.
12% of 60 would be 7.2, more than the actual raise of 6.
trick: Percent change always divides by the starting value: (new - old) / old.

q: A test score dropped from 80 to 60. % decrease?
why: The drop is 20 points from a starting score of 80: 20/80 = 25%.
traps: Reported the raw drop of 20 as the percent. Divide by the starting score, 80.
Divided by the new score (20/60). The base is where you started.
30% of 80 is 24, more than the actual drop of 20.
trick: Percent change always divides by the starting value: (new - old) / old.

q: A $50 lab fee is increased 8%. New cost?
traps: Treated 8% as 8 dollars.
Added 0.08 as a bare number. The 0.08 has to multiply the $50.
The fee went down. An increase adds.
trick: Turn the change into one multiplier: up 30% is x 1.30, down 30% is x 0.70.

why: Apply the changes one at a time, each to the current amount. $100 x 1.5 = $150. Then $150 x 0.5 = $75. The second percent is taken of $150, not of the original $100.
traps: Combined the two percents into one (+0% net) and applied it to the original. The second change acts on the new amount.
Applied only the second change to the original amount and skipped the first.
Stopped after the first change. The second change still has to be applied.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: A stock falls 30% then rises 30%. Net?
why: Multiply the factors: 0.7 x 1.3 = 0.91, which is 9% below the start. The rise is 30% of a smaller number than the fall was taken from.
traps: Assumed the changes cancel. The 30% rise is applied to only 70% of the start.
Right size, wrong direction. 0.91 is below 1.
Ignored the recovery entirely.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

why: Apply the changes one at a time, each to the current amount. $200 x 1.25 = $250. Then $250 x 1.25 = $312.50. The second percent is taken of $250, not of the original $200.
traps: Stopped after the first change. The second change still has to be applied.
Combined the two percents into one (+50% net) and applied it to the original. The second change acts on the new amount.
Not $200 x 1.25 x 1.25. After the first change the amount is $250; apply the second percent to that to get $312.50.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: If x − 9 = 4, what is the value of x?
why: x has 9 taken away, so add 9 to both sides: x = 4 + 9 = 13.
traps: Subtracted in the other order (9 - 4). Check: 5 - 9 = -4, not 4.
Subtracted 9 from 4. To undo 'minus 9' you add 9.
Multiplied 9 by 4. The operation to undo is a subtraction.
trick: Substitute your answer back into the original equation. It takes five seconds and catches sign slips.

q: If 4x − 5 = 11, what is the value of x?
why: Undo the operations in reverse order. First add 5 to both sides: 4x = 16. Then divide by 4: x = 4.
traps: Moved 5 across the equals sign without changing its sign.
Substitute it: 4(6) - 5 = 19, not 11.
Stopped at 4x = 16 and never divided by 4.
trick: Solve by undoing: clear the added or subtracted number first, then divide. Substitute your answer to check in five seconds.

q: If 5(2x − 4) = 30, what is the value of x?
why: Divide both sides by 5: 2x - 4 = 6. Add 4: 2x = 10. Divide by 2: x = 5.
traps: Substitute it: 5(6 - 4) = 10, not 30.
Substitute it: 5(14 - 4) = 50, not 30.
Substitute it: 5(4 - 4) = 0, not 30.
trick: Substitute your answer back into the original equation. It takes five seconds and catches sign slips.

q: A map's scale is 1 inch = 50 miles. Two cities are 4.5 inches apart. Real distance?
why: Each inch stands for 50 miles, so multiply: 4.5 x 50. Four inches is 200 miles and the half inch is 25 more: 225 miles.
traps: Multiplied 4.5 by 10. The scale is 50 miles per inch.
Divided 50 by 4.5. Inches times miles per inch gives miles.
Multiplied 4.5 by 100, double the real scale.
Rounded 4.5 up to 5 inches.
trick: A map scale is a unit rate: multiply the map distance by the real distance per unit.

q: If 8 oz of cheese costs $4.40, how much for 12 oz?
why: 12 oz is one and a half times 8 oz, so the price is 1.5 x $4.40 = $6.60. Unit-rate check: $4.40 / 8 = $0.55 per oz, and 12 x 0.55 = $6.60.
traps: Doubled the price. That would buy 16 oz.
That is the price of 10 oz at $0.55 each.
Used $0.50 per oz. The unit price is $0.55.
trick: Proportions: find the price of one unit, or scale by the ratio of the amounts.

q: A jet flies 540 miles in 1.5 hours. Average speed?
why: Speed = 540 / 1.5. In half an hour the jet covers a third of the distance, 180 miles, so in one hour it covers 360.
traps: Multiplied by 1.5. Speed divides distance by time.
Divided by 2 hours instead of 1.5.
trick: Let the units steer: miles per hour times hours leaves miles; miles divided by hours leaves miles per hour.

q: You drive 60 mph for 2 hr, then 40 mph for 3 hr. Average speed?
why: Average speed is total distance over total time. Distances: 60 x 2 = 120 and 40 x 3 = 120, total 240 miles. Time: 5 hours. 240 / 5 = 48 mph.
traps: Averaged the two speeds. More hours were spent at 40 mph, so the average leans below 50.
Too low. The trip is 240 miles in 5 hours.
Added the speeds. An average must fall between 40 and 60.
trick: Average speed = total distance / total time. Only average the speeds when the times are equal.

q: "The product of 4 and (n + 2) equals 24." Equation:
why: 'Product' means multiply, and the two things multiplied are 4 and the whole quantity (n + 2). The parentheses keep n + 2 together: 4(n + 2) = 24.
traps: Dropped the parentheses, so the 4 multiplies only n.
Multiplied all three. n + 2 is a sum that gets multiplied by 4 as one piece.
Used addition. 'Product' means multiply.
trick: 'The product of 4 and a quantity': wrap the quantity in parentheses before multiplying.

q: "Three times a number, decreased by 5, is 22." Equation:
why: 'Three times a number' is 3n. 'Decreased by 5' subtracts 5 from that result: 3n - 5 = 22.
traps: 'Decreased by' means subtract, not add.
Subtracted 5 from the number before tripling. The tripling comes first in the sentence.
Order reversed. The 5 is taken away from 3n.
trick: Find the base phrase first, then apply 'more than' or 'less than' to it. 'A less than B' reads backward: B - A.

q: "The sum of two consecutive integers is 47." Smaller integer:
why: Call them n and n + 1. Then 2n + 1 = 47, so 2n = 46 and n = 23. Check: 23 + 24 = 47.
traps: That is the larger of the pair. The question asks for the smaller.
trick: Consecutive integers are n, n + 1, n + 2. Reread which one the question wants.

q: What is the value of 2/3 × 4/5?
why: Multiply straight across: tops 2 x 4 = 8, bottoms 3 x 5 = 15, so the product is 8/15. No common denominator is needed for multiplication.
traps: Added tops and bottoms. Multiplication uses products: tops times tops, bottoms times bottoms.
Not 8/15. Tops multiply to 8 and bottoms multiply to 15.
Multiplied the tops but added the bottoms. Both parts get multiplied.
trick: Multiplying fractions: top times top over bottom times bottom, then reduce. Cancel common factors first to keep numbers small.

q: What is the value of 1/2 ÷ 1/4?
why: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip: 1/2 x 4/1. Tops 1 x 4 = 4, bottoms 2 x 1 = 2, so the quotient is 4/2, which reduces to 2.
traps: Multiplied without flipping the second fraction. Division needs the flip.
Flipped the first fraction instead of the second. Only the divisor gets flipped.
This is only the flipped second fraction. It still has to be multiplied by 1/2.
trick: Keep, change, flip: keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip the second.

q: What is the value of 3/8 × 2/9, written as a fraction in lowest terms?
What is the value of 5/6 ÷ 2/3?
why: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip: 5/6 x 3/2 = 15/12, which reduces to 5/4.
traps: Too small. Dividing 5/6 by 2/3, a number below 1, must make it bigger.
Multiplied without flipping the second fraction.
Equals 1/4, far too small. The quotient must be bigger than 5/6.
Flipped the first fraction instead of the second.
trick: Keep, change, flip: keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip the second.

q: What is the value of (2/3)(3/4)(5/6), written as a fraction in lowest terms?
What is the value of 0.4 + 0.35?
why: Line up the decimal points and add column by column: 0.4 + 0.35 = 0.75. Estimate check: about 0 + 0 = 0.
traps: Not 0.4 + 0.35. The exact value is 0.75; this is off by 0.36.
Not 0.4 + 0.35. The exact value is 0.75; this is off by 0.3465.
One tenth too low. Recheck the tenths column: the digits there give 0.75.
trick: Estimate with rounded numbers before you compute. The estimate catches a misplaced decimal point every time.

q: What is the value of 0.6 × 0.4?
why: Multiply as whole numbers, 6 x 4 = 24, then put back 2 decimal places (one for each digit after a decimal point in the factors): 0.24. Size check: multiplying two numbers below 1 gives something smaller than both.
traps: Decimal point one place too far right. Check the size against the numbers you started with.
Decimal point one place too far left. Check the size against the numbers you started with.
Not 0.6 x 0.4. The exact value is 0.24; this is off by 0.14.
trick: Estimate with rounded numbers before you compute. The estimate catches a misplaced decimal point every time.

q: What is the value of 1.5 ÷ 0.5?
why: 1.5 divided by 0.5 is about 3. Estimate first: 0.5 goes into 1.5 roughly 3 times, so only an answer near 3 makes sense.
traps: Decimal point one place too far left. A rough estimate (about 3) rules it out.
Decimal point one place too far right. A rough estimate (about 3) rules it out.
Multiplied instead of dividing.
trick: Estimate with rounded numbers before you compute. The estimate catches a misplaced decimal point every time.

q: What is the value of 0.025 × 800?
why: Multiply as whole numbers, 25 x 800 = 20000, then put back 3 decimal places (one for each digit after a decimal point in the factors): 20. Size check: multiplying 800 by a number below 1 must shrink it.
traps: Decimal point one place too far left. A rough estimate (about 20) rules it out.
Decimal point one place too far right. A rough estimate (about 20) rules it out.
Decimal point two places too far left.
trick: Estimate with rounded numbers before you compute. The estimate catches a misplaced decimal point every time.

q: Estimate 487 × 19. Closest answer:
why: Round to 500 x 20 = 10,000. Both numbers were rounded up, so the true product is a bit under 10,000. Of the choices, 9,000 is closest (the exact value is 9,253).
traps: Half the estimate. 500 x 10 would give this, but the second factor is about 20.
Too high. Even 500 x 20 is only 10,000.
A full power of ten too small.
trick: Round each factor to one leading digit, multiply, then nudge in the direction you rounded.

q: Estimate 12% of 837. Closest:
why: 10% of 837 is about 84, and 2% is about 17. Together that is about 100.
traps: That would be 12% of 1,000. 837 is noticeably less.
Just repeats the percent.
That is about 100% of the number.
trick: Estimate percents from 10% and 1%.

q: A bag of marbles is 78% red. If 412 marbles total, estimate red count.
why: Round to 80% of 400 = 320. (Exact: about 321.)
traps: That is nearly all the marbles. 78% leaves more than a fifth of them not red.
This is about the share that is not red (20% of 400).
That is about 10%.
trick: Round the percent and the total to friendly numbers before multiplying.

q: 25 × 16 = ? (mental)
why: 25 is 100 / 4, so 25 x 16 = 100 x 4 = 400. Four 25s make 100, and 16 holds four 4s.
traps: One zero short. 25 x 10 alone is already 250.
Tacked the 16 onto 400. The 16 is already used up.
This is 25 x 10. Six more 25s (150) are missing.
trick: Multiplying by 25: divide by 4, then multiply by 100.

q: 46 × 11 = ? (mental, ×11 trick)
why: 46 x 11 = 46 x 10 + 46 = 460 + 46 = 506. Digit shortcut: 4 + 6 = 10, so write 0 between the 4 and the 6 and carry 1 to the 4.
traps: Unchanged. Multiplying by 11 makes the number about eleven times larger.
Wrote a 5 in the middle without the carry. 4 + 6 is 10, so 0 goes in the middle and 1 carries.
Put the carried 1 in the middle and never added it to the front digit.
trick: Times 11: times 10, plus the number once more.

q: 35² = ? (squaring numbers ending in 5)
why: For a number ending in 5: multiply the tens digit by the next integer, 3 x 4 = 12, then attach 25. Result 1225. Check: 30 x 35 + 5 x 35 = 1050 + 175.
traps: That is 5 cubed. 35 squared is over 900, since 30 squared is 900.
Attached 25 to the original 35. The front part is 3 x 4 = 12.
Used 3 x 5 = 15 for the front. Multiply the tens digit by the next integer, 4.
trick: Squares ending in 5: (tens digit) x (tens digit + 1), then write 25.

q: Which of the following is equivalent to 3(x + 4)?
why: The 3 multiplies each term inside: 3 times x is 3x, and 3 times 4 is 12. Result: 3x + 12.
traps: Multiplied only the x. The 4 gets tripled too.
Multiplied only the 4. The x gets tripled too.
Added 3 to the 4 instead of multiplying.
trick: A number outside a parenthesis multiplies every term inside, sign included.

q: Which of the following is equivalent to −2(x − 5)?
why: Multiply each term by -2: -2 times x is -2x, and -2 times -5 is +10 (negative times negative is positive).
traps: Sign slip on the second term: -2 times -5 is positive 10.
Dropped the negative from the 2, which flips both signs.
The -5 was not multiplied by -2.
trick: A number outside a parenthesis multiplies every term inside, sign included.

q: Combine: 5x − 2x + 3 + x
why: Combine the x terms: 5 - 2 + 1 = 4, giving 4x. The 3 has no x, so it stays separate: 4x + 3.
traps: Dropped the constant 3.
Added all the x coefficients and ignored the minus sign on 2x.
Folded the 3 into the x terms. A plain number cannot merge with an x term.
trick: Only like terms combine. A lone x counts as 1x.

q: Which of the following is equivalent to 4(x + 2) − 3(x − 1)?
why: Distribute both: 4x + 8 and -3x + 3 (the -3 times -1 gives +3). Combine: 4x - 3x = x and 8 + 3 = 11.
traps: Sign slip: -3 times -1 is +3, not -3.
Added 3x instead of subtracting it.
The constants are 8 and +3, which make 11.
The constants were not multiplied by 4 and -3.
trick: A minus sign in front of a parenthesis flips every sign inside when you distribute.

q: What is the value of 3 + 4 × 2?
why: Multiply before adding: 4 x 2 = 8, then 3 + 8 = 11.
traps: Worked left to right: 3 + 4 = 7, then x 2. Multiplication goes first.
One short. The product 4 x 2 is 8, and 3 + 8 is 11.
Multiplied all three numbers and ignored the plus sign.
trick: Order: parentheses, exponents, multiply and divide, then add and subtract left to right.

q: What is the value of (2 + 3)² ÷ 5?
why: Parentheses first: 2 + 3 = 5. Exponent next: 5 squared = 25. Then divide: 25 / 5 = 5.
traps: Stopped before dividing by 5.
Broke up the parenthesis (2 + 25 / 5). The sum 2 + 3 must be finished before squaring.
This is 3 squared alone. The whole sum, 5, is what gets squared.
trick: Order: parentheses, exponents, multiply and divide, then add and subtract left to right.

q: What is the value of 10 − 3 × 2² + 1?
why: Exponent: 2 squared = 4. Multiply: 3 x 4 = 12. Then left to right: 10 - 12 = -2, and -2 + 1 = -1.
traps: Lost the negative. 10 - 12 is -2, so the result ends below zero.
Left the 2 unsquared: 10 - 6 + 1.
Subtracted before squaring: (10 - 6) squared, plus 1. The exponent belongs only to the 2.
trick: Order: parentheses, exponents, multiply and divide, then add and subtract left to right.

q: What is the value of −5 + 8?
why: Start at -5 on the number line and move 8 to the right: you pass 0 and land on 3. Same as 8 - 5.
traps: Added the sizes and kept the negative sign. The signs differ, so subtract the sizes: 8 - 5.
Added 5 and 8 as if both were positive.
Right size, wrong sign. The larger number, 8, is positive, so the result is positive.
trick: Different signs: subtract the sizes and keep the sign of the bigger one.

q: Which of the following gives every value of x that satisfies −2x < 6?
why: Divide both sides by -2 to isolate x. Dividing an inequality by a negative number reverses the direction, so less than becomes greater than: x > -3. Test x = 0: -2(0) = 0, which is less than 6, and 0 is in the answer.
traps: Divided by -2 but kept the sign pointing the same way. Dividing by a negative flips it. Test x = 0: it satisfies the original but not this.
Flipped the sign but lost the negative on the number: 6 divided by -2 is negative.
Two slips at once: the sign was not flipped and the negative on the number was lost. 6 divided by -2 is -3, and dividing by a negative reverses the direction.
trick: Any time you multiply or divide an inequality by a negative, flip the sign. Then test one easy number such as 0.

q: What is the value of −(−5)?
why: A minus sign means 'the opposite of'. The opposite of -5 is 5. Two negatives make a positive.
traps: Dropped one of the two negatives.
That would be -5 + 5. Nothing is being added here.
Doubled instead of taking the opposite.
trick: Read a leading minus as 'the opposite of'.

q: A pipe fills a tank in 4 hours. Another fills it in 6 hours. Together?
why: Add the rates: 1/4 + 1/6 = 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12 of the tank per hour. Flip for the time: 12/5 = 2.4 hours.
traps: Averaged the two times. Two pipes together must beat the faster pipe's 4 hours.
Added the times. More pipes make the job faster, not slower.
That would need two pipes that each take 4 hours. The second pipe is slower.
trick: Add rates, not times. For two workers: time together = product over sum, and it must beat the faster solo time.

q: Sam paints a wall in 3 hr. Lee in 5 hr. Together (per hour)?
why: Per hour, Sam paints 1/3 of the wall and Lee paints 1/5. Together: 1/3 + 1/5 = 5/15 + 3/15 = 8/15 of the wall per hour.
traps: Added the times (3 + 5) and flipped. Rates are added, not times.
Multiplied the two rates. Working together adds them.
Added tops and bottoms of 1/3 and 1/5 straight across.
trick: Add rates, not times. For two workers: time together = product over sum, and it must beat the faster solo time.

q: A inlet fills tank in 6 hr. Drain empties in 9 hr. With both open, time to fill?
why: The drain works against the inlet, so subtract rates: 1/6 - 1/9 = 3/18 - 2/18 = 1/18 of the tank per hour. Filling takes 18 hours.
traps: Subtracted the times (9 - 6). Subtract the rates instead.
Added the times.
Averaged the times. With a drain open, filling must take longer than the inlet's 6 hours alone.
Not the flip of 1/6 - 1/9. The net rate is 1/18 per hour.
trick: Opposing rates subtract. The net rate decides the time.

q: 40 oz of 25% acid mixed with 60 oz of 75% acid. Final concentration?
why: Acid amounts: 25% of 40 = 10 oz and 75% of 60 = 45 oz, total 55 oz. Total volume is 100 oz, so the mix is 55%.
traps: Plain average of 25 and 75. There is more of the 75% solution, so the result leans above 50.
Leans the right way but too far. Total acid is 55 oz in 100 oz.
Weights swapped: this pairs 60 oz with 25% and 40 oz with 75%.
trick: Mixtures are weighted averages: total solute over total volume. The answer falls between the two starting percents.

q: How much pure water to add to 50 oz of 30% saline to make 20% saline?
why: The salt does not change: 30% of 50 = 15 oz. For 15 oz to be 20% of the total, the total must be 15 / 0.20 = 75 oz. Water added: 75 - 50 = 25 oz.
traps: This is the amount of salt, not the water to add.
Adding 100 oz would give 15 / 150 = 10%.
Adding 30 oz would give 15 / 80, under 19%.
trick: Dilution: the solute stays fixed. Solve for the new total, then subtract the old total.

q: A store mixes 4 pounds of candy that costs $3 per pound with x pounds of candy that costs $5 per pound. The mixture costs $4 per pound. What is x?
why: $4 is exactly halfway between $3 and $5, so the two candies must be used in equal amounts: x = 4. Equation check: 12 + 5x = 4(4 + x) gives x = 4.
traps: Check: (12 + 10) / 6 is about $3.67, not $4.
Check: (12 + 40) / 12 is about $4.33, not $4.
trick: If the target is the midpoint of the two prices, the amounts are equal.

q: $1000 at 5% simple interest for 3 years. Final?
why: Simple interest earns the same amount each year on the original $1000: 5% of 1000 = $50. Three years gives $150. Final: $1150.
traps: One year of interest only.
This is the interest alone. Add the principal.
Used 50% in total. 5% for 3 years is 15%.
trick: Simple interest: final = principal x (1 + rate x years). Check whether the question wants the interest or the final balance.

q: $1000 at 10% compound annually for 2 years. Final?
traps: Simple interest: $100 each year. In year 2 the interest is on $1100, so it is $110.
Stopped after one year.
Added only $10 in year 2. 10% of $1100 is $110.
trick: Compound: multiply by (1 + rate) once per period. It always lands a bit above simple interest.

q: $2000 at 8% compounded quarterly for 1 year. Final ≈?
why: Quarterly compounding splits the 8% into four periods of 2%. The balance is multiplied by 1.02 four times: 2000 x 1.02^4 is about $2164.86, so about $2165. It must be slightly above the $2160 that 8% once would give.
traps: This is 8% applied once, with no compounding. Four 2% steps earn a little interest on interest.
Applied 4% in total, half the annual rate.
Too small an extra. Compounding adds about $4.86, not 50 cents.
Applied 12%. The annual rate is 8%, split into four 2% periods.
trick: Compounding n times a year: divide the rate by n and apply it n times.

q: Slope between (1,2) and (4,8)?
why: Rise: 8 - 2 = 6. Run: 4 - 1 = 3. Slope = rise / run = 6/3 = 2.
traps: This is only the run.
This is only the rise. Divide by the run.
Upside down: run over rise.
trick: Slope = (y2 - y1) / (x2 - x1). Keep the same point first on top and bottom, and y always goes on top.

q: Distance between (0,0) and (3,4)?
why: The horizontal leg is 3 and the vertical leg is 4. Pythagorean theorem: 9 + 16 = 25, and the square root of 25 is 5.
traps: Added the legs. The straight-line distance is the hypotenuse, shorter than walking both legs.
Forgot the square root at the end.
Averaged 3 and 4. The hypotenuse must be longer than either leg.
trick: Distance between points is a hidden right triangle. Watch for 3-4-5 and its multiples.

q: Midpoint of (2, 10) and (8, 4)?
why: Average the x values and the y values separately: (2 + 8)/2 = 5 and (10 + 4)/2 = 7.
traps: x is right, but the y average is (10 + 4)/2 = 7.
y is right, but the x average is (2 + 8)/2 = 5. 6 is the difference of the x values.
Added the coordinates and never divided by 2.
trick: Midpoint = the average of the x values and the average of the y values.

q: 30 mph in feet per second (1 mile = 5280 ft)?
why: 30 miles is 30 x 5280 = 158,400 feet. One hour is 3600 seconds. 158,400 / 3600 = 44 feet per second.
traps: Unchanged number. Both units changed, so the number must change.
That is 60 mph.
That is 15 mph.
Not 158,400 / 3600, which is exactly 44.
trick: Benchmark: 60 mph = 88 ft/s. Scale from there.

q: Convert 250 mL to liters.
why: 1000 mL make 1 L. Going to a bigger unit means fewer of them, so divide: 250 / 1000 = 0.25 L.
traps: Divided by 10. A liter is 1000 mL.
Divided by 100.
Multiplied by 10. Liters are bigger than mL, so the number shrinks.
Divided by 10,000, one place too far.
trick: Ask first: is the new unit bigger or smaller? Bigger unit, smaller number, so divide.

q: A solution is 0.5 g per mL. How much in 200 mL?
why: Each mL carries 0.5 g, so 200 mL carry 200 x 0.5 = 100 g. The mL cancel and grams remain.
traps: Half of 200 is 100, not 40.
Divided 0.5 by 200. More volume means more grams.
At half a gram per mL, the grams must come out below the 200 mL, not above.
trick: Rate times amount: write the units and cancel them like fractions.

q: P(at least one 6 in 3 dice)?
why: 'At least one' is easiest through the complement. P(no 6 on one die) = 5/6, so P(no 6 on all three) = (5/6) cubed. Subtract from 1.
traps: Added 1/6 three times. That double counts rolls with more than one 6; with 7 dice it would pass 1.
Same mistake in reduced form: 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6.
This is the chance of no 6 at all, the opposite event.
trick: At least one = 1 minus none. Compute the single 'none' case and subtract.

q: A coin is flipped 4 times. P(at least one heads)?
why: P(no heads) = P(all tails) = (1/2)^4 = 1/16. So P(at least one head) = 1 - 1/16 = 15/16.
traps: This is the chance of all tails. Subtract it from 1.
That is a single flip. Four tries make at least one head very likely.
This is the chance of exactly one head (4 positions out of 16 sequences).
trick: At least one = 1 minus none. Compute the single 'none' case and subtract.

q: Bag has 4 red, 6 blue. Draw 3 with replacement. P(at least one red)?
why: With replacement, each draw is not red with probability 6/10. All three not red: (6/10) cubed. At least one red is 1 minus that.
traps: This is the chance all three are red, a much narrower event.
This is the chance of no red at all, the opposite event.
Added 4/10 three times. A probability cannot exceed 1.
trick: At least one = 1 minus none. Compute the single 'none' case and subtract.

q: P(rolling 6 AND flipping heads)?
why: The die and the coin do not affect each other, so multiply: 1/6 x 1/2 = 1/12.
traps: Added the bottoms (6 + 2). Multiply the probabilities: the bottoms give 12.
This is the chance of a 6 or heads. The question says 'and'.
An 'and' of two events is rarer than either one, so it must be below 1/6.
trick: And (independent) = multiply, and the answer shrinks. Or = add, then subtract the overlap.

q: P(card is King OR Heart) from a 52-card deck?
why: 4 kings + 13 hearts = 17, but the king of hearts was counted in both groups. Remove the duplicate: 16 cards out of 52.
traps: Counted the king of hearts twice.
Hearts only. Three more kings qualify.
Kings only. Twelve more hearts qualify.
trick: Or: P(first) + P(second) - P(both). Skipping the subtraction double counts the overlap.

q: Two coins flipped. P(at least one heads)?
why: The four equally likely outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT. Three of them contain a head: 3/4. Or 1 - P(TT) = 1 - 1/4.
traps: That is one coin. A second coin gives another chance.
That is the chance of no heads (TT), or of two heads.
Tails on both is possible, so it is not certain.
trick: At least one = 1 minus none. Compute the single 'none' case and subtract.

q: Test is 95% accurate. Disease prevalence 1%. P(disease | positive)?
why: Picture 10,000 people. 100 are sick, and 95 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 healthy people, 5% test positive anyway: 495. Positives total 590, and only 95 are real: about 16%.
traps: This is the test's accuracy, P(positive given disease). The question asks P(disease given positive).
This is the share of people who are healthy.
This is the error rate, not the chance that a positive is real.
trick: For 'given a positive' questions, imagine a round number of people, count each group, and divide the group you want by the total that fits the condition.

q: A bag has 5 red, 5 blue. Draw 2 without replacement. P(2nd red | 1st red)?
why: After one red is removed, 4 reds remain among 9 marbles: 4/9.
traps: That is the chance before anything was drawn. One red is gone and so is one marble.
Lowered the total to 9 but forgot that a red was removed too.
Same as 5/10: ignores the first draw.
trick: Without replacement: after each draw, lower both the count of that color and the total.

q: 70% of students study. 90% of studiers pass. 30% of non-studiers pass. P(studied | passed)?
why: Out of 100 students: 70 study and 63 of them pass; 30 do not study and 9 of them pass. Passers total 72, and 63 studied: 63/72 = 87.5%.
traps: This is the share who study before you know who passed. Passing is evidence of studying, so it goes up.
This is P(pass given studied), the reverse of what is asked.
Too low. 63 of the 72 passers studied.
trick: For 'given a positive' questions, imagine a round number of people, count each group, and divide the group you want by the total that fits the condition.

q: Committee of 3 from 10. How many ways?
why: A committee has no positions, so order does not matter. Ordered picks: 10 x 9 x 8 = 720. Each committee shows up in 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 orders: 720 / 6 = 120.
traps: This counts ordered lineups. The same three people in a different order are the same committee.
Multiplied 10 by 3. Counting uses the chain 10 x 9 x 8.
Not 720 / 6. Each pick removes one person, so the chain is 10 x 9 x 8, then divide by 6.
trick: Ask whether swapping two picks makes a new outcome. Yes: multiply a falling chain. No: also divide by the orderings.

q: How many 4-letter "words" using A,B,C,D,E (no repeats)?
why: Order matters in a word. Choices per position: 5, then 4, then 3, then 2. 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 120.
traps: This is the count if order did not matter (which letter to leave out).
This is 5^4, which lets letters repeat.
This is 4 x 3 x 2 x 1, the ways to order four fixed letters. It ignores which letter is left out.
This is 5 x 4 x 3, only three positions filled.
trick: Ask whether swapping two picks makes a new outcome. Yes: multiply a falling chain. No: also divide by the orderings.

q: Pick 2 boys from 5 and 3 girls from 6. How many groups?
why: Boys: 5 x 4 / 2 = 10 pairs. Girls: 6 x 5 x 4 / 6 = 20 trios. Every pair can go with every trio, so multiply: 10 x 20 = 200.
traps: Added 10 and 20. Selections made together multiply.
Multiplied 5 by 3. Each group needs its own combination count.
Added 5 and 6.
trick: Separate selections made together: count each, then multiply.

q: How many real solutions: 2x² + 3x + 5 = 0?
why: Discriminant: b^2 - 4ac = 9 - 4(2)(5) = 9 - 40 = -31. A negative discriminant means the parabola never touches the x-axis: no real solutions.
traps: One solution needs a discriminant of exactly 0. Here it is -31.
Two solutions need a positive discriminant. Here it is -31.
A quadratic has at most 2 solutions.
trick: Compute b^2 - 4ac first: positive means 2 real solutions, zero means 1, negative means none.

q: How many real solutions: x² − 4x + 4 = 0?
why: Discriminant: 16 - 16 = 0, so there is exactly one solution. Factoring shows it too: (x - 2)^2 = 0 gives only x = 2.
traps: Two different solutions need a positive discriminant. Here it is 0, and both factors give the same x = 2.
No solutions needs a negative discriminant.
A quadratic has at most 2 solutions.
trick: Compute b^2 - 4ac first: positive means 2 real solutions, zero means 1, negative means none.

q: For x² − 6x + k = 0 to have 2 real solutions, k must be?
why: Two real solutions need a positive discriminant: 36 - 4k > 0. That gives 4k < 36, so k < 9.
traps: Inequality reversed. Large k makes 36 - 4k negative, which means no real solutions.
That makes the discriminant exactly 0: one repeated solution, not two.
The cutoff is 9, not 0. For example k = 10 gives a negative discriminant.
trick: Compute b^2 - 4ac first: positive means 2 real solutions, zero means 1, negative means none.

q: Boat 30 mph downstream, 20 mph upstream, same distance. Avg speed?
why: Pick a distance, say 60 miles each way. Down takes 2 hours, up takes 3 hours: 120 miles in 5 hours = 24 mph. Formula: 2(30)(20) / (30 + 20) = 24.
traps: Averaged the speeds. More time is spent on the slow leg, so the true average is below 25.
Above the midpoint. The slow leg lasts longer, which pulls the average down, not up.
Too low. Total distance over total time gives 24.
Close, but total distance over total time gives exactly 24.
trick: Equal distances at two speeds: never average the speeds. Use total distance over total time (or 2ab / (a + b)).

q: Round trip: 60 mph one way, 40 mph back. Avg speed?
why: Say each leg is 120 miles. Out takes 2 hours, back takes 3: 240 miles in 5 hours = 48 mph.
traps: Averaged the speeds. The 40 mph leg takes longer, so the average sits below 50.
Added the speeds. An average must fall between 40 and 60.
Too low. 240 miles in 5 hours is 48.
trick: Equal distances at two speeds: never average the speeds. Use total distance over total time (or 2ab / (a + b)).

q: Drove 60 mph for 1 hr, then 40 mph for 1 hr. Avg speed?
why: Here the times are equal, so the plain average works. Distance: 60 + 40 = 100 miles in 2 hours = 50 mph.
traps: That is the result for equal distances. Here equal hours are spent at each speed.
This is the total distance, not the speed.
Too low. 100 miles in 2 hours is 50.
This is just the slower speed.
trick: Equal times: average the speeds. Equal distances: do not.

q: Mean = 100, σ = 15. Value of 130 has z-score?
why: 130 is 30 above the mean. Each standard deviation is 15, so 30 / 15 = 2 standard deviations above.
traps: Raw distance from the mean. Divide by the standard deviation.
This is the standard deviation itself.
One standard deviation above would be 115.
trick: z = (value - mean) / standard deviation.

q: Normal: μ=50, σ=10. P(value > 60)?
why: 60 is one standard deviation above the mean. About 68% of values fall within one standard deviation, leaving 32% outside, split evenly: 16% above and 16% below.
traps: That is the share above the mean (50), not above 60.
That is the share within one standard deviation, between 40 and 60.
That is both tails together. Only the upper tail is asked for.
trick: 68-95-99.7: sketch the bell, mark the cutoff, and split the leftover between the two tails.

q: Mean=100, σ=10. P(value between 80 and 120)?
why: 80 and 120 are each 20 from the mean, which is 2 standard deviations. About 95% of a normal distribution lies within 2 standard deviations.
traps: That is within 1 standard deviation (90 to 110).
That is within 3 standard deviations (70 to 130).
That is everything on one side of the mean.
trick: 68-95-99.7: sketch the bell, mark the cutoff, and split the leftover between the two tails.

q: Triangle with base 8 and height 4 has area:
why: Area of a triangle is half of base times height: (1/2)(8)(4) = 16.
traps: Forgot the one half. Base times height is the full rectangle.
Added base and height.
Not half of 32. Base times height is 32, and half of that is 16.
trick: A triangle is half of the rectangle around it: (1/2) x base x height.

q: Three triangles share base AB and have apexes on a line parallel to AB. Largest area?
why: Area depends only on base and height. All three share base AB, and every point on a line parallel to AB is the same distance from it, so the heights match too. Same base and height means same area.
traps: Shape does not matter. Sliding the apex along the parallel line changes the angles but not the height.
No apex is taller. A line parallel to AB stays the same distance from it.
A right angle does not add area. Only base and height count.
trick: Same base, apex anywhere on a parallel line: same area.

q: Right triangle, legs 6 and 8. Hypotenuse?
why: Pythagorean theorem: 36 + 64 = 100, and the square root of 100 is 10. This is the 3-4-5 triangle doubled.
traps: Added the legs. The hypotenuse is always shorter than the two legs combined.
Averaged the legs. The hypotenuse is the longest side, so it must exceed 8.
12 squared is 144, not 100.
trick: Know the 3-4-5 family (6-8-10, 9-12-15) on sight.

q: Cube side length 5. Volume?
why: Volume = side cubed = 5 x 5 x 5 = 125.
traps: One face's area. Multiply by 5 once more.
Multiplied 25 by 3 instead of by 5.
Multiplied the side by 3 instead of cubing it.
trick: Volume fills space, so it uses three lengths multiplied. Area uses two.

q: If a cube's side doubles, volume becomes:
why: Volume uses three lengths multiplied. Doubling each one gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times the volume.
traps: Only one dimension was doubled. All three sides double.
That is what happens to area (two dimensions). Volume has three.
One factor of 2 too many.
trick: Scale every length by k: areas scale by k squared, volumes by k cubed.

q: Sphere radius 3. Volume = (4/3)πr³. Approx (use π≈3)?
why: r cubed = 27. (4/3) x 27 = 36. Multiply by pi, taken as 3: 108.
traps: Stopped before multiplying by pi.
This is r squared. Volume needs r cubed, then 4/3 and pi.
Pi was already replaced by 3 to reach 108, so it cannot appear again.
trick: Sphere volume is (4/3) pi r cubed. Cube the radius first, then deal with 4/3 and pi.

q: Q: What is x? (1) x + 5 = 12. (2) x² = 49. Sufficient?
why: Statement (1) gives x = 7, one value, so it is sufficient. Statement (2) gives x = 7 or x = -7, two values, so it is not.
traps: x squared = 49 allows both 7 and -7. Two possible values is not sufficient.
No need to combine. Statement (1) already pins x down without help.
Statement (1) is a one-step equation with a single solution.
trick: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone first, then together. A squared equation usually hides two values.

q: Q: Is x positive? (1) x² = 9. (2) x > −2.
Q: What is the area of the rectangle? (1) Length is 4. (2) Perimeter is 14.
why: Area needs length and width. (1) gives only the length. (2) gives 2L + 2W = 14, which many rectangles satisfy. Together: L = 4, so W = 3 and the area is 12.
traps: Length without width leaves the area open.
A perimeter of 14 fits 1 by 6, 2 by 5, 3 by 4 and more, each with a different area.
Together they fix both sides: 4 and 3.
trick: Data sufficiency: test each statement alone first, then together. A squared equation usually hides two values.

q: What is the value of 2³ × 2⁴?
why: Same base, multiplying: add the exponents. Three 2s times four 2s is seven 2s: 2^7.
traps: Multiplied the exponents. That rule is for a power raised to a power.
Multiplied the bases as well. The base stays 2.
Subtracted the exponents. That is the division rule.
trick: Same base: multiply means add exponents, divide means subtract exponents.

q: Which of the following is equivalent to (3²)⁴, written as a single power of 3?
What is the value of 5⁰?
why: Any nonzero number to the power 0 is 1. Reason: 5^2 / 5^2 = 5^0 by the subtraction rule, and anything divided by itself is 1.
traps: That is 5^1.
The exponent is 0, but the value is 1. Using 5 as a factor zero times leaves the starting 1.
trick: Zero exponent gives 1; negative exponent gives one over.

q: If |x| = 5, what are the possible values of x?
why: |x| = 5 asks which numbers are 5 units from zero. There are two: 5 and -5.
traps: Only half the solution. -5 is also 5 units from zero.
Only half the solution. 5 is also 5 units from zero.
|0| is 0, not 5.
trick: An absolute value equation usually has two solutions, one on each side.

q: Which of the following gives every value of x that satisfies |x − 3| < 2?
why: Read it as: x is less than 2 units away from 3. That is everything between 3 - 2 = 1 and 3 + 2 = 5.
traps: That is the solution of |x - 3| > 2, the values far from 3. 'Less than' keeps x close.
Only the upper bound. x = -10 fits this but is 13 away from 3.
Only the lower bound. x = 100 fits this but is 97 away from 3.
trick: |x - a| < b means within b of a (one interval). |x - a| > b means farther than b (two outside pieces).

q: Which of the following gives every value of x that satisfies |x + 1| > 4?
why: x + 1 is the same as x - (-1), so this says x is more than 4 units from -1. Go 4 left of -1 to reach -5 and 4 right to reach 3. The solution is everything outside: x < -5 or x > 3.
traps: That is the inside, the solution of |x + 1| < 4.
Only the right-hand piece. Values such as -10 also work.
Wrong direction: x = 0 fits this, but |0 + 1| = 1 is not greater than 4.
trick: |x - a| < b means within b of a (one interval). |x - a| > b means farther than b (two outside pieces).

q: You're solving a problem cold (no timer). What's the right move?
opts: Take your time, get it right
why: Untimed practice exists to build the method. With no clock running, accuracy is the only thing being trained, so work each step fully.
traps: Speed comes after accuracy. Rushing a method you have not learned just rehearses mistakes.
Skipping removes the practice you need most. With no timer there is no cost to staying.
Guessing teaches nothing when no clock is forcing it.
trick: Learn it slow, then make it fast.

q: You've spent 90 seconds on a question with no progress. What's the move?
why: The section gives 45 minutes for 40 questions, a little over a minute each. After 90 seconds with no progress the question has already used more than its share, and every question is worth the same. Mark it, move on, and come back with whatever time is left.
traps: More time on a stalled problem is taken from questions you can solve.
A blind guess with no mark gives up the chance to return with fresh eyes.
One hard question says nothing about the rest.
trick: No progress at 90 seconds: mark it, move on, and return at the end.

q: You skipped 4 questions. You have 2 minutes left. Best move?
why: There is no penalty for a wrong answer on the DAT, so a blank is the only sure zero. Two minutes over four questions is 30 seconds each: enough to rule out a choice or two and pick, not enough to solve fully.
traps: Solving one fully can eat the whole two minutes and leave three blanks.
A fixed letter ignores what you can rule out. Even one elimination beats a blind pick.
Random picks waste the 30 seconds you have to eliminate.
trick: Eliminate, then guess. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

q: You're guessing on a 4-choice question with no idea. What's your best play?
opts: Eliminate any obviously wrong, then guess
why: No points are lost for a wrong answer, so always answer. Ruling out even one choice raises your odds: 1 in 4 becomes 1 in 3.
traps: A fixed letter is a blind guess. It cannot use anything you know.
Random guessing skips the cheap step of removing choices that cannot be right.
A skipped question scores zero for certain. A guess has a chance.
trick: Eliminate, then guess. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

q: You're educated-guessing under time pressure. Two answers seem possible. What gives you the edge?
You finished 12 untimed problems in 18 min. 3 wrong. What matters most for next session?
why: Nine of twelve right means three gaps. Finding out whether each miss was a concept, a setup or an arithmetic slip tells you exactly what to fix; more speed would only repeat the same misses faster.
traps: Speed does not repair the reason for a miss.
Pacing practice assumes the method is already reliable, and 3 misses in 12 says it is not yet.
Stopping leaves the three gaps in place.
trick: Every miss gets a reason: concept, setup, or arithmetic.

q: Mid-untimed-set, you realize the question type is unfamiliar. Best move?
opts: Pause, re-read the lock + worked example
why: An unfamiliar type means the method is missing, and untimed mode is the place to learn it. Going back to the lesson and its worked example gives you a method to copy.
traps: A guess leaves the gap where it is.
Skipping the whole skill guarantees it stays unfamiliar on test day.
A timer adds pressure but no knowledge.
trick: Learn it slow, then make it fast.

q: Untimed mode. You got 7/10 on a skill. Should you advance to 90s pacing?
opts: Yes, time pressure will sharpen you

q: A store marks a $40 item up 25%, then discounts the new price by 20%. What is the final price?
why: $40 x 1.25 = $50, and $50 x 0.80 = $40. A 25% rise followed by a 20% cut returns to the start because 1.25 x 0.80 = 1. Adding the percentages (+25 - 20 = +5%) gives $42.

q: How many skips per 45-min DAT QR section is healthy?
After skipping, when do you return?
opts: End of section, with remaining time
why: First collect every point you can get quickly. Marked questions come last, so they only spend time that is left over.
traps: Coming straight back spends time before the easier points are banked.
Halfway through, there are still unseen questions that may be quicker points.
A marked question still counts, and there is no penalty for answering it.
trick: No progress at 90 seconds: mark it, move on, and return at the end.

q: You're 30 min in, 25 of 40 questions done, no skips yet. Pace check?
What is the 90-second rule?
opts: 90s with no progress, mark and skip
why: It is a limit on being stuck, not a pace. If 90 seconds pass and you have no path to an answer, mark the question and move on. The section allows about 67 seconds per question on average, so 90 seconds is already over budget.
traps: It is not a timer for skipping on a schedule. Questions you are solving should be finished.
It is a ceiling for stuck questions, not a target. Most questions should take less.
The whole section lasts 45 minutes.
trick: No progress at 90 seconds: mark it, move on, and return at the end.

q: 5-choice question. You eliminated 1. Should you guess or skip?
why: With one choice gone, four remain, so a guess is right 1 time in 4. A blank is right 0 times, and wrong answers cost nothing.
traps: Skipping scores zero for certain. Picking takes a second.
A fixed letter might be the very choice you just eliminated.
Not a real strategy. Choose among the four choices still standing.
trick: Eliminate, then guess. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

q: A recipe uses 2.5 cups of flour for 10 cookies. How many cups of flour are needed for 36 cookies?
why: Flour per cookie is 2.5/10 = 0.25 cup, so 36 cookies need 36 x 0.25 = 9 cups. 14.4 comes from dividing 36 by 2.5 instead of scaling.

q: Eliminate-before-guess: how does it improve odds on a 5-choice question?
why: A blind guess among five choices is right 1 time in 5. Remove two and you are choosing among three: 1 in 3.
traps: Each choice removed raises the odds: 20%, 25%, 33%, 50%.
Elimination improves the odds; it does not guarantee the answer.
You may or may not remove the trap. The gain comes from having fewer choices left.
trick: Eliminate, then guess. There is no penalty for a wrong answer, so never leave a blank.

q: A numerical answer feels suspiciously round (exactly 100, exactly 1/2). On a multi-step calculation. What does it suggest?
opts: Often a trap on multi-step QR

q: What is the value of 5/12 + 1/4?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 12: 5/12 stays as it is and 1/4 = 3/12. Add the tops: 5 + 3 = 8, giving 8/12, which reduces to 2/3.
traps: Added the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get added.
Too small by 17/48 compared with the true value 2/3. Redo the conversion to a denominator of 12 and combine only the tops.
Too small by 1/12 compared with the true value 2/3. Redo the conversion to a denominator of 12 and combine only the tops.
Put both over 12 but kept the old tops. When the bottom is scaled up, the top has to be scaled by the same factor.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 7/10 − 2/5?
why: Fractions can only be combined when the pieces are the same size, so put both over 10: 7/10 stays as it is and 2/5 = 4/10. Subtract the tops: 7 - 4 = 3, giving 3/10.
traps: Subtracted the tops and the bottoms straight across. Denominators are piece sizes; they never get subtracted.
Put both over 10 but kept the old tops. When the bottom is scaled up, the top has to be scaled by the same factor.
Added tops and bottoms straight across, and the problem is a subtraction.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6?
traps: Stopped after the first two fractions and never added 1/6.
Too big. The tops are 3 + 2 + 1 = 6, not 11.
Added all tops and all bottoms straight across.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 4 1/2 − 1 3/4?
why: Use quarters: 4 1/2 = 4 2/4. You cannot take 3/4 from 2/4, so borrow 1 whole: 3 6/4 - 1 3/4 = 2 3/4.
traps: Subtracted the fractions backward (3/4 - 1/2) and never borrowed.
Subtracted only 3/4 and forgot the whole 1.
Borrowed correctly, but the fraction part is 6/4 - 3/4 = 3/4.
trick: If the top fraction is smaller, borrow 1 from the whole number before subtracting.

q: What is the value of 2/3 + 5/6 − 1/2?
traps: One sixth too big. 1/2 is 3/6, so the tops are 4 + 5 - 3 = 6.
One sixth too small. 2/3 is 4/6, so the tops are 4 + 5 - 3 = 6.
The tops total 6 over 6, which is exactly 1, not 3/4.
trick: Same-size pieces first: convert to a common denominator, then combine only the numerators.

q: What is the value of 5/6 × 3/10, written as a fraction in lowest terms?
What is the value of 2/3 ÷ 4/9?
why: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip: 2/3 x 9/4. Tops 2 x 9 = 18, bottoms 3 x 4 = 12, so the quotient is 18/12, which reduces to 3/2.
traps: Multiplied without flipping the second fraction. Division needs the flip.
Added tops and bottoms. Division means multiply by the flipped second fraction.
This is only the flipped second fraction. It still has to be multiplied by 2/3.
trick: Keep, change, flip: keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, flip the second.

q: What is the value of (1/2) × (2/3) × (3/4), written as a fraction in lowest terms?
How many 1/4-cup servings in 2 cups?
why: How many quarters fit in 2? Each cup holds 4 quarter-cups, so 2 cups hold 8. As division: 2 / (1/4) = 2 x 4 = 8.
traps: Multiplied 2 by 1/4. 'How many fit' is a division.
That is the number of servings in one cup.
That is the number of cups, not servings.
trick: Keep, change, flip: dividing by 1/4 is multiplying by 4.

q: What is the value of (3/4) ÷ (1/2) ÷ (3/8)?
why: Work left to right, flipping each divisor. 3/4 x 2/1 = 3/2. Then 3/2 x 8/3 = 24/6 = 4.
traps: Multiplied all three fractions with no flips.
Too small. Dividing 3/4 by two fractions below 1 must make it bigger each time.
Flipped both divisors but dropped the 3/4.
Divided the last two fractions first. Division runs left to right.
trick: A chain of divisions runs left to right; flip every fraction after the first.

q: What is 18% of 200?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 18% of 200 is 0.18 x 200 = 36. Mental route: 10% of 200 is 20, and 1% is 2; build 18% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 200.
180 is 90% of 200, not 18%. Anchor on 10% of 200 = 20.
Decimal point one place too far right. Check: 10% of 200 is only 20.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 150% of 80?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 150% of 80 is 1.5 x 80 = 120. Mental route: 10% of 80 is 8, and 1% is 0.8; build 150% from those.
traps: Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 80.
80 is 100% of 80, not 150%. Anchor on 10% of 80 = 8.
530 is 662.5% of 80, not 150%. Anchor on 10% of 80 = 8.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 4% of 25?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 4% of 25 is 0.04 x 25 = 1. Mental route: 10% of 25 is 2.5, and 1% is 0.25; build 4% from those.
traps: 25 is 100% of 25, not 4%. Anchor on 10% of 25 = 2.5.
Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 25.
Multiplied 4 by 25 and never divided by 100. 4% is 0.04 as a decimal.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: What is 0.5% of 600?
why: Percent means per hundred, so 0.5% of 600 is 0.005 x 600 = 3. Mental route: 10% of 600 is 60, and 1% is 6; build 0.5% from those.
traps: Decimal point one place too far right. Check: 10% of 600 is only 60.
Multiplied 0.5 by 600 and never divided by 100. 0.5% is 0.005 as a decimal.
Just repeats the percent. It still has to be applied to 600.
Decimal point one place too far left. Check: 10% of 600 is already 60.
trick: Find 10% (move the decimal one place) and 1% (two places), then build any percent from those.

q: A solution is 12% salt. 250g of solution contains how much salt?
why: 12% of 250 g: 10% is 25 g and 2% is 5 g, total 30 g.
traps: 120 g would be nearly half the solution. 12% is closer to a tenth.
Subtracted 12 from 250. The 12 is a percent, not grams.
Just repeats the percent. That would be right only for 100 g of solution.
trick: Find 10% and 1%, then build any percent from those.

q: A textbook is marked up 40% to $98. What was original price?
why: The new price is 140% of the original: original x 1.4 = 98. Divide: 98 / 1.4 = 70. Check: 40% of 70 is 28, and 70 + 28 = 98.
traps: Took 40% off $98. The 40% was a share of the original price, not of $98.
Marked $98 up another 40%. The original must be below $98.
trick: Working backward from a percent change: divide by the multiplier. Do not reverse the percent.

q: $80 lab fee dropped to $60. What % decrease?
why: The drop is $20 on a starting fee of $80: 20/80 = 25%.
traps: Raw drop of 20 reported as a percent. Divide by the starting $80.
This is what remains (60/80), not the decrease.
Divided by the new fee (20/60). The base is the original.
trick: Percent change always divides by the starting value: (new - old) / old.

q: Tuition went from $5,000 to $5,750. % increase?
traps: This is the new tuition as a percent of the old. The increase is the part above 100%.
Divided by the new tuition (750/5750). The base is the original.
Reported the dollar change as a percent.
trick: Percent change always divides by the starting value: (new - old) / old.

q: A stock at $50 needs to grow to $75. What % gain?
why: The gain needed is $25 on a starting price of $50: 25/50 = 50%.
traps: Reported the dollar gain as a percent.
This is the new price as a percent of the old (75/50).
Divided by the target price (25/75). The base is the starting price.
trick: Percent change always divides by the starting value: (new - old) / old.

q: A measurement reads 18% high. True value if measured as 295?
why: Reading 18% high means measured = true x 1.18. So true = 295 / 1.18 = 250. Check: 18% of 250 is 45, and 250 + 45 = 295.
traps: Went up instead of down. A reading that runs high means the true value is lower.
Subtracted 18 as a plain number. It is 18% of the true value.
The true value must be below the reading, since the reading runs high.
trick: Working backward from a percent change: divide by the multiplier. Do not reverse the percent.

why: Apply the changes one at a time, each to the current amount. $200 x 1.1 = $220. Then $220 x 1.1 = $242. The second percent is taken of $220, not of the original $200.
traps: Stopped after the first change. The second change still has to be applied.
Combined the two percents into one (+20% net) and applied it to the original. The second change acts on the new amount.
Not $200 x 1.1 x 1.1. After the first change the amount is $220; apply the second percent to that to get $242.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: A price was raised 30%, then dropped 10%. Net change?
why: Multiply the factors: 1.30 x 0.90 = 1.17, a net rise of 17%. The 10% cut is taken from the higher price, so it removes 13 points, not 10.
traps: Added the percents (30 - 10). The 10% applies to 130% of the start.
Added 30 and 10 as if both were increases.
Treated both as decreases.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

why: Apply the changes one at a time, each to the current amount. $500 x 0.6 = $300. Then $300 x 1.4 = $420. The second percent is taken of $300, not of the original $500.
traps: Combined the two percents into one (+0% net) and applied it to the original. The second change acts on the new amount.
Not $500 x 0.6 x 1.4. After the first change the amount is $300; apply the second percent to that to get $420.
Applied only the second change to the original amount and skipped the first.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: A salary was cut 20%, then raised 25%. Net?
why: 0.80 x 1.25 = 1.00. The raise is 25% of a smaller salary, which exactly restores the 20% that was cut.
traps: Added the percents (25 - 20). The two percents have different bases.
Treated both as increases.
Treated both as decreases.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: $100 increased by 50% three times. Final?
why: Multiply by 1.5 three times: 100, 150, 225, 337.50.
traps: Added $50 three times. Each 50% is taken of the new, larger amount.
A little high. The steps are 150, 225, 337.50.
Only one increase applied.
trick: Successive percents multiply. Write each as a multiplier and chain them; never add the percents.

q: If 3x − 5 = 2x + 8, what is the value of x?
why: Subtract 2x from both sides: x - 5 = 8. Add 5: x = 13.
traps: Subtracted 5 from 8 instead of adding it. Moving -5 across makes it +5.
Sign error. Substitute: the left side would be -44 and the right side -18.
Substitute it: left side -2, right side 10. Not equal.
trick: Substitute your answer back into the original equation. It takes five seconds and catches sign slips.

q: If 7 − 2x = 1, what is the value of x?
why: Subtract 7 from both sides: -2x = -6. Divide by -2: x = 3. Check: 7 - 6 = 1.
traps: Lost a negative when dividing -6 by -2. Check: 7 - 2(-3) = 13, not 1.
Check: 7 - 8 = -1, not 1.
Stopped at 2x = 6. Divide by 2.
trick: Substitute your answer back into the original equation. It takes five seconds and catches sign slips.

q: If (2x + 3)/5 = 3, what is the value of x?
why: Multiply both sides by 5: 2x + 3 = 15. Subtract 3: 2x = 12. Divide by 2: x = 6.
traps: Stopped at 2x = 12.
Added 3 instead of subtracting it. Check: (18 + 3)/5 = 4.2, not 3.
trick: A fraction bar groups the whole numerator. Clear the denominator before touching what is on top.

q: If 3(x − 2) − 2(x + 1) = 7, what is the value of x?
why: Distribute: 3x - 6 - 2x - 2 = 7. Combine: x - 8 = 7. Add 8: x = 15.
traps: Sign slip: -2 times +1 is -2, so the constants are -6 - 2 = -8, not -4.
trick: A minus sign in front of a parenthesis flips every sign inside when you distribute.

q: If 4x + 7 = 2(x − 3) + 19, what is the value of x?
why: Distribute: 4x + 7 = 2x - 6 + 19 = 2x + 13. Subtract 2x: 2x + 7 = 13. Subtract 7: 2x = 6, so x = 3.
traps: Stopped at 2x = 6.
Check: left side 7, right side 13. Not equal.
Multiplied only the x by 2 (2x - 3 + 19). The 2 also multiplies the 3.
trick: Substitute your answer back into the original equation. It takes five seconds and catches sign slips.

q: A 2:5 oil-to-vinegar dressing. To make 70 mL total, how much oil?
why: 2 + 5 = 7 parts. 70 mL / 7 = 10 mL per part. Oil is 2 parts: 20 mL.
traps: Divided 70 by 5. The total is split into 7 parts.
Halved the total. Oil is 2 of 7 parts, less than half.
That is the vinegar (5 parts).
trick: Ratios: add the parts, find the size of one part, then multiply by the parts you need.

q: A 1:9 tincture (drug:carrier). Patient needs 4 mL of drug. Total volume?
why: Drug is 1 part of 1 + 9 = 10 total parts. If 1 part is 4 mL, the total is 10 x 4 = 40 mL.
traps: That is the carrier alone (9 parts). The total includes the drug.
Added 1 to 4. Each part is 4 mL, and there are 10 parts.
This is the carrier's ratio number, not a volume.
